Newborn Care

Oesophageal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula: newborn care and follow-up

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Oesophageal atresia (EA) interrupts the food pipe between the mouth and stomach. A tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) is an abnormal connection between the food pipe and windpipe; the two often occur together. A newborn with excessive frothy saliva, choking or breathing trouble needs immediate medical assessment. Blue or grey lips or tongue, pauses in breathing, very fast or difficult breathing or inability to wake are emergencies.

How the food pipe and airway are affected

Normally, swallowed milk passes through the oesophagus to the stomach, while air travels down the trachea to the lungs. In EA, the upper oesophagus usually ends in a blind pouch. Saliva or milk can collect and enter the airway; a fistula can also allow stomach contents into the lungs and air into the stomach. Aspiration, lung inflammation or infection and inadequate oxygen can be serious.

EA/TEF is uncommon and may occur alone or with other birth differences. Diagnosis and repair can be lifesaving, but surgery does not promise that every child will have completely normal swallowing or breathing. Continuing specialist care matters even when the initial repair goes well.

The five anatomical patterns

Type A is atresia without a fistula: both oesophageal ends are blind. Type B has a fistula from the upper segment to the trachea and a blind lower segment. Type C, the commonest pattern, has a blind upper segment and a fistula between the lower segment and trachea. The upper pouch and the lower connection create different routes for aspiration.

Type D has both upper and lower fistulas alongside atresia. Type E, also called H-type fistula, has a continuous oesophagus without atresia but an abnormal connection to the trachea. Milk may reach the stomach in H-type disease, so it can be recognized later. These patterns guide investigation and surgery; percentages vary between series and do not predict an individual child’s outcome.

Signs at birth and respiratory complications

Excessive drooling or white frothy saliva, repeated coughing or choking with feeds, milk returning and breathing distress can appear soon after birth. A baby may develop rapid breathing, nasal flaring or blue or grey colour when oxygen is low. Recurrent chest infections or feeding-related cough can reveal a previously unrecognized H-type fistula. Do not give another feed to test whether the baby can swallow.

Tracheomalacia means that the windpipe is too floppy and narrows during breathing. It can cause a harsh or barking cough, noisy breathing, difficulty clearing secretions, choking or serious breathing pauses. It needs individualized airway assessment; not every cough after repair is harmless or caused by tracheomalacia. New or worsening respiratory symptoms need review.

Associated conditions, causes and genetic advice

Around half of affected babies have additional abnormalities, such as heart defects, kidney or urinary-tract differences, vertebral or limb abnormalities, or another digestive blockage, including an imperforate anus. VACTERL describes an association of vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb findings; it is not a single genetic diagnosis. Other neurological or developmental concerns are assessed when present.

The cause is often unknown. Early development, genetic changes and other factors may contribute; this is not evidence that a parent caused the condition. Some children have a recognizable condition, such as CHARGE, Feingold syndrome, SOX2-related disorder, Fanconi anaemia or a chromosome abnormality. Clinical genetics can tailor testing and recurrence advice to the child and family. A single low recurrence percentage does not apply to every syndrome or family.

Prenatal suspicion and diagnosis after birth

A small or unseen stomach and excess amniotic fluid on ultrasound may raise prenatal suspicion, but neither is specific, and a normal scan does not exclude EA/TEF. Specialist ultrasound and sometimes fetal MRI can clarify selected cases. If suspected, the maternity and neonatal teams plan birth where appropriate newborn and paediatric surgical care can be provided.

After birth, a trained clinician may gently pass a feeding tube and take chest and abdominal X-rays. A tube coiled in the upper pouch supports EA; abdominal gas can suggest a lower fistula. The tube must not be forced or tested at home. A tube reaching the stomach does not exclude H-type fistula. Bronchoscopy and selected specialist contrast studies can locate a fistula and assess the airway; routine contrast into a blind upper pouch risks aspiration.

Assessment and stabilization before repair

Echocardiography checks heart defects and the position of the aortic arch, which can affect surgical planning; it does not prevent a defect. The team also checks kidneys, urinary tract, spine, limbs and anus, with further investigations guided by findings. Neonatology, paediatric surgery and anaesthesia coordinate care with cardiology, respiratory, gastroenterology, feeding and nutrition specialists as needed.

Until a safe feeding plan is established, the hospital usually avoids oral feeds, drains pooled saliva from the upper pouch with a specialist suction tube and provides fluids and nutrition by an appropriate route. Breathing support, pain care and antibiotics around surgery or for suspected infection are clinician-managed. Families should not insert or adjust suction or feeding tubes, give trial feeds or withhold needed respiratory support themselves.

Surgery and long-gap oesophageal atresia

Repair usually closes the fistula and joins the oesophageal ends when feasible. An open chest operation or thoracoscopic surgery may be chosen according to anatomy, the baby’s stability and available expertise. Many babies are repaired early, but there is no universal 24-to-48-hour deadline or identical operation for every baby. Prematurity, major heart disease, lung illness and a large gap can change the plan.

With long-gap EA, the ends cannot initially be joined safely. Expert centres generally aim to preserve the child’s own oesophagus, using delayed joining after growth or selected traction/lengthening procedures. Nutrition may require a gastrostomy while waiting. In selected cases, replacement using stomach or intestine is considered, with different risks and long-term effects. Timing may extend over months; parents should discuss options, second opinions and specialist-supervised oral-skill support rather than attempt feeds or tube manipulation at home.

Recovery, feeding and outlook

After surgery, a baby may need neonatal intensive care, ventilation, pain relief, drains and tube or intravenous nutrition. Oral feeding starts according to the repair, swallowing and airway assessment, not a fixed day. Some children need ongoing tube feeds and feeding therapy. Discharge depends on a safe individualized plan and caregiver training, not a guaranteed one-to-two-week stay or universal full oral feeding.

Many children survive and develop well with modern care, but outlook depends on anatomy, prematurity, birth weight, major heart or genetic conditions, respiratory health and access to specialist care. Historical groups based on a 1,500-gram weight threshold and cardiac defects describe risk rather than a personal survival guarantee. Families need an explanation of their baby’s actual situation, not a fixed promise of complete cure.

Long-term follow-up and everyday care

The repaired oesophagus may move food poorly, and reflux, narrowing at the join, swallowing difficulty, recurrent chest infections, anastomotic leakage or a recurrent fistula may require investigation. A symptomatic narrowing may need specialist dilation, sometimes more than once. Reflux treatment, texture changes, feeding therapy, airway treatment or further surgery are tailored to findings. Do not start, stop or change prescribed treatment without the team.

Structured follow-up should continue through childhood and adolescence into adult services, covering growth, nutrition, swallowing, breathing and quality of life. Ask for a written feeding and emergency plan, tube-care teaching where relevant and infant first-aid/resuscitation training. Routine infant sleep remains on the back on a firm, flat, clear surface, including with reflux; do not raise the cot, use wedges or choose side/front sleep yourself. Any medically necessary exception requires an explicit specialist plan.

When symptoms need urgent help

Get emergency help immediately if a baby or child under five has any one of these signs: swelling of the lips, tongue or throat with trouble swallowing or talking; very fast or difficult breathing, including grunting or the chest or tummy pulling in; breathing pauses; blue, grey, pale or mottled skin, lips or tongue; skin that feels cold or clammy; a rash that does not fade under pressure; temperature of 38°C or above before three months, or 39°C or above at three to six months; temperature below 36°C, feeling cold or shivering; a weak, unusually high-pitched or continuous cry; fainting, loss of consciousness or difficulty waking; no urine for 12 hours; or a seizure. On darker skin, colour changes may be easier to notice on the palms or soles. One sign is enough: do not wait for the others, and seek immediate help if you think the child is seriously unwell even without a listed sign. Choking with inability to breathe also needs immediate emergency action; follow the dispatcher’s instructions and trained infant first aid. Do not assume that a known fistula, reflux or a familiar cough makes these signs safe to watch at home.

A newborn with persistent frothy saliva, repeated feed-related choking or suspected inability to swallow needs immediate assessment and no further trial feeds. If none of the emergency signs applies, seek urgent same-day advice for new feeding difficulty or refusal to feed, recurrent choking, fever or feeling unusually hot, unusual lethargy, reduced urine or dehydration, worsening cough, persistent vomiting or inability to keep fluids down, green, yellow, bloody or projectile vomit, blood in the stool, a swollen or tender tummy, diarrhoea lasting over a week, or crying that does not settle with marked distress. A baby under three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs immediate emergency assessment. Follow the surgical team’s more specific instructions and do not wait for several signs to occur together.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC and specialist information distinguish oesophageal interruption from an airway fistula, including H-type disease without atresia. Prenatal imaging can suggest the condition but cannot exclude all cases; postnatal tube/X-ray and airway assessment are performed by trained teams.

ERNICA expert consensus supports specialized long-gap care, preference for preserving the native oesophagus when feasible, parental training and structured lifelong multidisciplinary follow-up. The operation, timing, feeding support and surveillance are individualized.

Genetic resources describe both isolated and syndromic disease and family-specific inheritance. NHS infant guidance supports flat back sleeping even with reflux and immediate action for serious breathing, colour, responsiveness or young-infant fever warnings.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record appointments, feeding instructions, medicines and questions for the specialist team. It cannot diagnose EA/TEF, interpret imaging, select an operation or establish that feeding or breathing is safe. The empty incubator image illustrates specialist newborn care and shows no child or diagnostic finding.

When to seek help

A newborn with frothy saliva, choking or suspected swallowing obstruction needs immediate medical assessment; do not give another feed to test swallowing or force a tube. Get emergency help immediately if a baby or child under five has any one of these signs: swelling of the lips, tongue or throat with trouble swallowing or talking; very fast or difficult breathing, including grunting or the chest or tummy pulling in; breathing pauses; blue, grey, pale or mottled skin, lips or tongue; skin that feels cold or clammy; a rash that does not fade under pressure; temperature of 38°C or above before three months, or 39°C or above at three to six months; temperature below 36°C, feeling cold or shivering; a weak, unusually high-pitched or continuous cry; fainting, loss of consciousness or difficulty waking; no urine for 12 hours; or a seizure. On darker skin, colour changes may be easier to notice on the palms or soles. One sign is enough: do not wait for the others, and seek immediate help if you think the child is seriously unwell even without a listed sign. Choking with inability to breathe also needs immediate emergency action; follow the dispatcher’s instructions and trained infant first aid. Follow the specialist feeding and emergency plan; do not manipulate tubes or change treatment yourself.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • EA interrupts the oesophagus; TEF connects it abnormally to the airway. H-type fistula can occur without atresia.
  • Frothy saliva, choking or respiratory trouble in a newborn needs immediate assessment. Blue or grey lips or tongue, breathing pauses or inability to wake are emergencies.
  • Diagnosis includes specialist tube/X-ray assessment, airway evaluation and checks for associated abnormalities; no home feeding or tube test is safe.
  • Repair, long-gap techniques, feeding and discharge are individualized. Surgery is not a guarantee of completely normal swallowing or breathing.
  • Ongoing multidisciplinary care supports growth, feeding, airway health and transition to adult care. Use a written emergency plan and safe infant sleep.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between EA and TEF?

EA means the oesophagus is interrupted; TEF means there is an abnormal connection to the windpipe. They often coexist. H-type TEF has a continuous oesophagus without atresia, so a feeding tube may pass to the stomach and diagnosis may be later.

What signs are most concerning in a newborn?

Excessive frothy saliva, choking with feeds and breathing difficulty need immediate assessment, without another trial feed. Blue or grey lips or tongue, breathing pauses, very fast or difficult breathing, fainting, loss of consciousness or inability to wake need immediate emergency help.

Can an ultrasound diagnose it before birth?

Ultrasound may show excess amniotic fluid or a small or absent stomach, but these findings are not specific. Normal prenatal imaging cannot exclude every type. Specialist ultrasound or selected fetal MRI may help planning; many cases are confirmed after birth.

How is the diagnosis confirmed after birth?

Clinicians use a gently passed tube and chest/abdominal X-rays when EA is suspected. Bronchoscopy and selected specialist studies assess fistula anatomy and airway problems. A tube reaching the stomach does not rule out H-type TEF. Parents must not force a tube or give feeds as a diagnostic test.

Does every baby need the same operation immediately?

No. The fistula is closed and the oesophagus joined when safe, using an approach chosen by the specialist team. A long gap, prematurity, heart defects or illness can require staged treatment and nutritional support. Delayed joining or other reconstruction may take months.

Is this inherited, and will it happen in another pregnancy?

Many cases are sporadic and the cause is unknown, while others occur with a genetic or chromosome condition. Genetic testing and recurrence counselling depend on the baby’s findings and family history. A universal recurrence percentage would be misleading.

Will surgery cure all feeding and breathing difficulties?

Not always. Many children do well, but reflux, impaired oesophageal movement, narrowing, recurrent fistula or tracheomalacia may need ongoing treatment. Growth, feeding, swallowing and respiratory follow-up should continue into adult care. Prognosis is individual.

What should caregivers learn before discharge?

Ask for a written feeding, medicine, tube-care and emergency plan and infant first-aid training. Do not adjust tubes or trial unsafe feeds yourself. Keep routine sleep flat on the back on a firm clear surface; do not use a cot incline or wedge for reflux. Breathing pauses, blue or grey lips or tongue or inability to wake require emergency help.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
